respuesta.lectura: He cares about being able to buy the house without draining his emergency fund, while not cutting back on his retirement. What will move him most is seeing how many months of expenses his cash covers. He will also react strongly to how long his savings last.
respuesta.porque_orden: Liquidity and the house first, then retirement; we close with the score and good news on the credit card

colchon.q: If your income stopped tomorrow, how many months of expenses do you think your cash covers?
colchon.mas: That's more months than you said ({tu})
colchon.siente: Michael, your cash covers **3.2 months** of essential expenses. The recommended reserve is 5 to 6 months; if you set aside your short-term goals, the months covered drop to **0**.
colchon.salida: Work out with your advisor how the house and the emergency fund fit together

jubilacion.q: Do you have enough to retire at 58 and live on it?
jubilacion.siente: Michael, according to the plan your savings run out at **age 85**, while your goal is to retire at 58. Guaranteed income covers 34% of projected spending.
jubilacion.salida: Draw less from your savings in retirement

nota.q: From 0 to 100, what Financial Health score do you think your plan gives you?
nota.mas: That's more points than you said ({tu})
nota.menos: That's fewer points than you said ({tu})
nota.siente: Your score today is **26 out of 100**, Michael. It sums up that the order of your money (house, emergency fund, savings) needs sorting out.
nota.salida: Increase the growth-oriented part of your investments

tarjeta_interes.q: You pay $200 a month on your credit card. How much of that goes to interest?
tarjeta_interes.mas: More goes to interest than you said ({tu})
tarjeta_interes.siente: Of your $200 a month, **$58** goes to interest. That portion slows down paying off the balance and the monthly relief.
tarjeta_interes.salida: Talk to your advisor to prioritize payments and look at options
